title: The Infant Who Overturned a Cart
story:
A cart is a heavy thing, made to carry pots and grain and the whole weight of a household's goods. It does not fall over on its own. And yet, on the day of a certain child's birth-rites in Gokula, a loaded cart overturned for no reason anyone could see, and the only one near it was an infant too small to lift a single one of its pots.

The day had begun with ceremony. Yasoda, Nanda's wife, had bathed and purified herself, and the brahmins had come to recite the benedictions over her newborn son and had been honored with gifts. The women of Vraja had gathered for the rite of the child's first rising, and Yasoda moved among them, greeting each one, for a mother performing such a ceremony has many duties and her mind was full of them. In the press of it all, the child was set down for a moment in the shade of a cart that stood in the courtyard, heaped with vessels.

He was hungry, perhaps, or simply tired of being still. He began to cry, and as infants do when they cry, he kicked.

One small foot struck the underside of the cart above him. A foot as soft and tender as a new leaf, as a fresh sprout of the season, striking wood and iron.

The cart went over. Not tipped gently, but overturned, its wheels wrenched from the axle and its shaft and yoke broken, its vessels spilled and shattered across the courtyard.

The crash brought everyone running. Yasoda came, and the women of Vraja, and Nanda and the other men, and they stood around the wreckage in a ring of wonder, agitated by a sight they could not explain. How, they asked one another, could a cart turn over by itself? No wind had stirred. No animal had been near it. There it lay, upended and broken, and in the middle of it all sat the child, crying.

The cowherd boys and girls, who had been playing close by, said what they had seen. The child did it, they said. It was the baby who kicked it, with his own foot. But the grown men shook their heads. That was child-talk, the sort of thing children invent. How could an infant's foot overturn a cart that strong men could hardly shift?

Yasoda did not stay to argue. She was afraid, afraid of the evil eye and of whatever unkind influence might be drawn toward a child who had been part of such a wonder. She gathered up her crying son and held him to her.

The cowherds, strong men all, set the cart upright again and gathered up what remained of its goods. Then Nanda, troubled and unable to explain what had happened, did what a father does when the world will not give an answer. He gathered the brahmins skilled in the mantras and had the protective rites recited over his son, with the words of the three Vedas, and he brought out his finest cows and adorned them with cloth and garlands and gold, and stood with a steady heart while the blessings were spoken over the child.

But no prayer could undo what the courtyard had seen that day, and no one who was there could forget it. A cart overturned by the kick of a child too small to lift a single one of its pots, and the child himself, unhurt, reaching up to be held. The men went back to their herds and the women to their houses, but the question went with them, unasked and unanswered.
reflection: The wonder of the episode is not only the overturned cart but the way the village receives it: the children tell the plain truth and the adults refuse it, because the truth is too large for their idea of what a child can do.
tradition_note: The Harivamsha sets this episode while Yasoda is away bathing at the river and Nanda returns from the forest to find the cart overturned; the Bhagavata Purana places it during the child's birth-rites. The miracle at the heart of both is the same.
next_story_tease: Kamsa's servants were not finished with Gokula, and the next would come not in a human shape but as a storm.
hero_scene: The infant Krishna lies beneath an overturned cart, one small foot raised in a kick, while the cart's wheels lie torn away and pots and vessels scatter across the courtyard as the cowherd men and women stare in astonishment.
